---
title: "How to carry out a Genome-Wide Association Study"
subtitle: "A decision-focused, reproducible guide using pancreatic cancer as a worked example"
---

::: {.callout-note title="About this guide"}
This is the companion website to the methodology manuscript developed within the
**TRANSPAN COST Action (CA21116), Working Group 1**; the target journal is to be defined. It pairs
annotated **PLINK 2** and **R** code with a fully open, reproducible demo dataset, and is written
for master's students, clinicians and early-career researchers **without** a bioinformatics
background.
:::

## What is a GWAS?

A genome-wide association study (GWAS) tests the statistical **association** between
**genetic variants**, typically single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), and a **trait**
across the entire genome, in order to identify genetic factors that contribute to complex
traits and diseases.

## Why pancreatic cancer?

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is the deliberate case study throughout this guide:
a **relatively rare, multifactorial cancer** with a poorly characterised genetic component.
Single-centre studies are underpowered, and international consortia, such as PanScan, PanC4 and
PANDoRA, are the rule rather than the exception. Teaching GWAS under these realistically difficult
conditions makes the methodological decisions more transparent than a large, well-powered textbook
example would: a correctly executed pipeline does not, on its own, guarantee a genome-wide
significant result, and this guide is built to show why.

## Who this guide is for

The tutorial is written for two kinds of reader:

- **Beginners**, with little or no previous experience of GWAS, bioinformatics or the command
  line. Every command is given in full, together with the output you should expect to see.
- **Intermediate and advanced users**, who already work with genetic data and want a transparent,
  reproducible teaching workflow in which each decision is visible rather than buried in a
  wrapper.

## How to use this guide

Every analysis step is shown as a real command you can run yourself on the open demo dataset. The
sections released so far take you from raw genotypes through quality control, population
structure, association testing, meta-analysis and fine mapping; the remaining steps are added as
each is completed.

👉 **Start here:** [Before you start, setup and your first PLINK command](getting_started.qmd)

::: {.callout-tip title="No coding experience?"}
You do **not** need to know how to program. Every command is given in full, with an explanation
of what it does and what the output should look like. If you can copy, paste and press Enter,
you can follow this guide.
:::

The structure is intentionally step by step. Some tasks are split across more than one script even
where they could be merged into a single command, because the purpose is to make each decision
visible and to let you see what each filter actually removed.

For the same reason, this is not a high-performance computing workflow and it is not a template
for large-scale parallel processing. If you are working with a full consortium dataset, run the
same steps in an appropriate computing environment and distribute jobs according to your
institution's guidelines.
